vessel.name: Wright Flyer (1903)

facts.Fate: wrecked by a gust after flight 4; Smithsonian since 1948

vessel.history: The Flyer made all four of its flights on 17 December 1903 from level ground near the brothers' camp at Kill Devil Hills, launched from a rail laid into a wind of more than 20 mph.
vessel.story: Orville's first flight lasted 12 seconds. Wilbur's fourth flight of 59 seconds was the longest; minutes later strong gusts blew the machine over and wrecked it.

routes.history: On 17 December 1903 Orville and Wilbur Wright made four flights in the Wright Flyer at Kill Devil Hills, about 4 miles south of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina: the first sustained flights of a manned, powered and controlled heavier-than-air aircraft.
routes.story: The Smithsonian at first refused to credit the Wrights, and Orville threatened to send the Flyer to London. It went on display at the Smithsonian on 17 December 1948, 45 years to the day after its flights.

voyages.record: First day of scheduled US Air Mail

vessel.name: Curtiss JN-4HM 'Jenny' (US Army Air Service)
vessel.history: US Air Mail began on 15 May 1918 with six converted Army Curtiss JN-4HM 'Jenny' biplanes flown by Army pilots on the Washington–Philadelphia–New York route.
vessel.story: On the first day Lt George Boyle, just out of flight school, flew the northbound leg from Washington, got lost and made a forced landing near Waldorf, Maryland, 18 minutes after take-off.

routes.history: The Post Office Department made Air Mail a new class of service on 15 May 1918, with the Washington–Philadelphia–New York route and the first special Air Mail stamps. Army pilots flew it at first; the route was the first step towards a transcontinental air mail.
routes.story: Lt James Edgerton, just out of flight school, flew the Philadelphia–Washington leg on the first day; the northbound flight from Washington got lost and came down near Waldorf, Maryland.

routes.history: Scheduled transcontinental air mail between New York and San Francisco began on 8 September 1920. At first mail flew by day and went by train at night; full day-and-night service began on 1 July 1924, so a coast-to-coast trip that had taken over 70 hours was scheduled at 34 h 46 min westbound. Congress funded a lighted airway along the route in 1923; the 2,665-mile New York–San Francisco airway was completed to a June 1925 deadline.
routes.story: On 22 February 1921 Jack Knight flew the Omaha–Chicago leg at night for the first time. By 1 September 1927 all US air mail, including the transcontinental route, was flown under contract by commercial carriers.

routes.history: Aéropostale was founded in Toulouse on 25 December 1918 as the Lignes Aériennes Latécoère ('La Ligne') and operated until 1933. Jean Mermoz opened Toulouse–Barcelona over the Pyrenees in 1924, and in 1926 a leg was added from Casablanca across the Sahara to Dakar, where mail went on by steamer to South America.
routes.story: The first nonstop Toulouse–Saint-Louis (Senegal) flight began in 1927. Antoine de Saint-Exupéry managed and flew for its Aeroposta Argentina subsidiary; his novel about those years became the 1933 film Night Flight.

voyages.record: First nonstop South Atlantic air mail crossing

vessel.name: Latécoère 28 seaplane (Jean Mermoz)
vessel.history: On 12–13 May 1930 the Aéropostale pilot Jean Mermoz made the first nonstop air crossing of the South Atlantic with mail, from Dakar to Natal.
vessel.story: Before this, mail reaching Dakar by air went on to South America by steamer; Aéropostale had flown Rio de Janeiro–Natal since November 1927.

routes.history: On 12–13 May 1930 Aéropostale finally flew the South Atlantic: Jean Mermoz took a float-equipped Latécoère 28 nonstop from Dakar to Natal, 3,058 km in 19 h 35 min, with 122 kg of mail.
routes.story: Until then mail from France flew to Dakar and crossed the ocean by steamer; Aéropostale had flown Rio de Janeiro–Natal since November 1927, so the flight joined the two halves of La Ligne.
